name: Portuguese (Brazilian)
variety: Educated urban Brazilian Portuguese of the south-east (São Paulo, the variety of the JIPA illustration), with notes on Rio de Janeiro
sources: Barbosa, Plínio A. and Albano, Eleonora C. (2004). Brazilian Portuguese. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 34(2), 227-232.
Mateus, Maria Helena and d'Andrade, Ernesto (2000). The Phonology of Portuguese. Oxford University Press.
Cristófaro Silva, Thaïs (1999). Fonética e fonologia do português: roteiro de estudos e guia de exercícios. São Paulo: Contexto.
Bisol, Leda (ed.) (1996). Introdução a estudos de fonologia do português brasileiro. Porto Alegre: EDIPUCRS.

Escudero, Paola; Boersma, Paul; Rauber, Andréia Schurt; Bion, Ricardo A. H. (2009). A cross-dialect acoustic description of vowels: Brazilian and European Portuguese. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 126(3), 1379-1393.
Frota, Sónia and Vigário, Marina (2001). On the correlates of rhythmic distinctions: the European/Brazilian Portuguese case. Probus 13, 247-275.
Moraes, João Antônio de (1998). Intonation in Brazilian Portuguese. In Hirst and Di Cristo (eds.), Intonation Systems: A Survey of Twenty Languages. Cambridge University Press.
Frota, Sónia; Cruz, Marisa; et al. (2015). Intonational variation in Portuguese: European and Brazilian varieties. In Frota and Prieto (eds.), Intonation in Romance. Oxford University Press.

vowel_formants.speaker: adult male, São Paulo (means over speakers, stressed oral vowels)
vowel_formants.formants: two values per vowel, F1 and F2; the source does not report F3, and it covers only the seven stressed oral vowels

contrasts: seven oral vowels under stress /i e ɛ a ɔ o u/, five before the stress /i e a o u/, three in final unstressed position [ɪ ɐ ʊ]
oral versus nasal vowels (lá versus lã) and oral versus nasal diphthongs (pau versus pão)
tap /ɾ/ versus strong r /x/ between vowels (caro versus carro)
four sibilants /s z ʃ ʒ/ in onsets, one sibilant in the coda
[tʃ dʒ] are mostly predictable variants of /t d/ before [i], but contrast marginally in loanwords and names (tchau, Djalma)
allophony: /t d/ are affricates [tʃ dʒ] before [i], [ĩ] and [ɪ], including the [ɪ] that comes from final unstressed 'e' and the epenthetic vowel: tia [ˈtʃiɐ], dia [ˈdʒiɐ], leite [ˈlejtʃɪ], cidade [siˈdadʒɪ]; parts of the north-east and south keep plain stops
coda /l/ is vocalised to [w]: mal [maw], Brasil [bɾaˈziw], alto [ˈawtʊ], sol [sɔw]; onset /l/ is a clear alveolar lateral
final unstressed /e o a/ are [ɪ ʊ ɐ], short and often devoiced after voiceless consonants; pretonic vowels keep their quality (pequeno [peˈkenʊ])
strong r (word-initial, written rr, after n, l, s) is a back fricative [x], [χ] or [h], voiced [ɣ] or [ɦ] before voiced consonants; an alveolar trill is regional (south)

coda r varies by region: a tap [ɾ] in the city of São Paulo, a fricative [x] or [h] in Rio de Janeiro and the north, a retroflex approximant [ɻ] in the interior of São Paulo and neighbouring states; final r of infinitives is often dropped
the coda sibilant is [s] or [z] (by voicing of the next sound) in São Paulo and most of the country, [ʃ] or [ʒ] in Rio de Janeiro
a stressed vowel before a nasal onset is nasalised and /a/ is raised: cama [ˈkɐ̃mɐ], banana [baˈnɐ̃nɐ]

nasal vowels are followed by a brief nasal consonant before stops (campo [ˈkɐ̃mpʊ]); before fricatives and word-finally there is none (longe [ˈlõʒɪ], fim [fĩ]); final '-em' is [ẽj̃] (bem [bẽj̃]), final '-om' often [õw̃]
/ɲ/ is usually a nasalised palatal glide [j̃] (banho [ˈbɐ̃j̃ʊ]); /ʎ/ is often [lʲ] or [lj]
an epenthetic [i] breaks up clusters that the syllable structure does not allow: ritmo [ˈxitʃimʊ], advogado [adʒivoˈɡadʊ], pneu [piˈnew], psicologia [pisikoloˈʒiɐ]
before ɾ, ʃ, ʒ the diphthong /ej/ is often [e] (peixe, feira) and /ow/ is generally [o] (ouro)
in Rio de Janeiro and elsewhere a glide is inserted before a final sibilant in stressed syllables (mas [majs], três [tɾejs])
syllable_structure: (C)(C)V(G)(C), with the coda limited to a sibilant, /ɾ/ (strong or weak by region), the glide from /l/, or nasality
phonotactics: onset clusters are stop or /f/ plus /ɾ/ or /l/; all other clusters receive an epenthetic [i]
word-final consonants of loanwords also take a final [i] (clube, Facebook [fejsiˈbukɪ])
/ɾ/, /ɲ/ and /ʎ/ do not begin native words
vowels in hiatus across words are fused or the first becomes a glide

stress.type: lexical, restricted to the last three syllables
stress.rule: Stress is penultimate in words ending in a, e, o (also with s, m, ns), final in words ending in l, r, z, i, u, a nasal vowel or a diphthong, and elsewhere it is marked by an accent in the spelling.
stress.cues: duration first, then intensity and pitch; vowel quality distinguishes stressed from post-tonic vowels ([ɪ ɐ ʊ]) but pretonic vowels stay full; secondary stresses alternate leftwards from the main stress

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: only final unstressed vowels are reduced, to [ɪ ɐ ʊ]; pretonic vowels are full; epenthetic [i] adds syllables
rhythm.notes: Frota and Vigário (2001), using the proportion of vocalic intervals and the variability of consonantal intervals, find mixed rhythm with syllable-timed and mora-timed properties, clearly different from European Portuguese. Escudero et al. (2009) found stressed vowels longer in Brazilian than in European Portuguese.

length.notes: No length contrast. Stressed vowels are clearly longer than unstressed ones, and final unstressed vowels are the shortest.

intonation.declarative: a rising accent on nearly every content word before the nucleus (L+H* or L*+H, peak on or after the stressed syllable), then a fall to low on the last stressed syllable (H+L*) and a low boundary
intonation.yes_no_question: same word order as the statement; low stretch before the nucleus, a rise on the last stressed syllable and a fall on the syllables after it (rise-fall, L+H* L%); when the stressed syllable is final the fall is cut short
intonation.wh_question: high on the question word at the start, gradual fall, low on the last stressed syllable and low boundary
intonation.continuation: rise on the last stressed syllable of the phrase with a high boundary
intonation.accent_shape: prenuclear L+H*: low at the start of the stressed syllable, peak at its end or in the next syllable; nuclear H+L* in statements
intonation.notes: Moraes (1998); Frota et al. (2015). Brazilian Portuguese has a pitch accent on almost every prosodic word, unlike the Lisbon standard.

phonation: final unstressed vowels are often devoiced after voiceless consonants and before pause

problems: final '-em', '-ens' is an oral diphthong plus a velar nasal [eɪŋ] (bem, tem, homem, também, viagem) instead of the nasal diphthong [ẽj̃]; 'ãe' has an oral glide [ɐ̃j]

every nasal vowel is followed by a nasal consonant segment, also before fricatives and at the end of a word (longe [lˈõnʒɪ], ênfase [ˈẽnfɐzɪ], fim [fˈĩŋ], bom [bˈõm]), where the language has a plain nasal vowel or a nasal glide
no epenthetic [i] in consonant clusters: ritmo [xˈitmʊ], advogado [ˌadvoɡˈadʊ], pneu [pnˈeʊ], psicologia [psˌikoloʒˈiɐ] (the rule option for epenthesis is reserved for the MBROLA voices)

coda r is always a tap and coda s always [s] or [z] (São Paulo pattern); there is no setting for the fricative coda r or the [ʃ] coda of Rio de Janeiro, and the strong r labelled [x] is synthesised with the glottal [h] sound
/ɲ/ is a full palatal nasal stop, not the nasal glide [j̃] usual in Brazil
the first syllable of longer words always gets secondary stress (pequeno [pˌekˈenʊ], cidade [sˌidˈadʒɪ]) whatever the distance to the main stress
intonation uses one of the generic tune sets (voice option 'intonation 2'): the rise-fall on the last stressed syllable of yes-no questions and the rising accent on each content word are not modelled
good: t and d are affricated before [i] and before final unstressed 'e' (tia, dia, leite, cidade, de, antigo)
coda l is vocalised (mal [mˈaʊ], sol [sˈɔw], Brasil, alto, último)
final unstressed e and o are raised to [ɪ] and [ʊ] while pretonic vowels stay full
stressed vowels before a nasal onset are nasalised and raised (cama [kˈɐ̃mɐ])
the nasal vowels and the diphthongs [ɐ̃w̃], [õj̃], [ũj̃] are present; open and close mid vowels are distinguished with a large exception list

notes: The voice is marked mature and is the better developed of the two Portuguese voices. Regional variation in Brazil is large for coda r, coda s and the palatalisation of t and d; a single setting cannot cover it.
